title: Maritime NDT Consulting & Class Audit Support, Brownsville
description: Level III support for Brownsville yards and NDT firms: new-owner NDT programs, recycling and tow inspections, UR Z17 gauging approval. Tell us your audit.
h1: Maritime NDT Consulting and Class Audit Support in Brownsville, Texas
html:
At the Port of Brownsville, vessels are fabricated, repaired and, more than anywhere else in the country, taken apart, and each of those trades brings a different reviewer to the NDT records. This page is for yard managers, fabrication shops, gauging firms and inspection companies in the Rio Grande Valley who need their NDT program ready for a class, owner or customer audit, or who are building a program from scratch under new ownership. Atlantis NDT provides ASNT NDT Level III consulting for that work; tell us what you are preparing for.

A port where ships are built, rebuilt and recycled

Brownsville is the center of US ship recycling. Three recyclers at the port, All Star Metals, International Shipbreaking Limited (part of EMR) and SteelCoast, together handle more than 85 percent of US Navy and Maritime Administration ship recycling, according to the port authority. The decommissioned aircraft carrier Kitty Hawk arrived in May 2022, the sixth Navy carrier brought to Brownsville for recycling, and the carrier John F. Kennedy has since made its final voyage there as well.

The port's best-known building and repair yard is going through a change of hands. Seatrium, which absorbed Keppel's offshore and marine business and ran the yard as Seatrium AmFELS, formerly Keppel AmFELS, announced in September 2025 that it had agreed to sell the facility to Karpower Valley LLC, part of the Karpowership group. Completion depended on closing conditions including the port authority transferring the lease, and Seatrium said it would finish its ongoing projects at the yard by the end of 2025. Around the port there are also fabrication shops serving offshore, industrial and energy construction, and large LNG export construction along the ship channel has pulled inspection contractors into the area.

For NDT, that mix produces three very different situations: a yard re-forming its quality program under a new owner, recycling work where inspection is occasional but consequential, and construction and repair work where owners and class societies audit inspection firms in the ordinary way.

When a yard changes owners, NDT credentials stay behind

A new owner usually inherits a site, cranes, drydocks and, often, many of the same skilled people. What it does not inherit is the paperwork that made those people and processes acceptable to auditors. Expect each of these to need re-establishing:

  • Class approvals. A society's approval of a service supplier or a works approval names the company that was audited. A new legal entity has to apply and be audited in its own name.
  • Management system certification. ISO 9001 and similar certificates are issued to an organization and scope; a successor company needs its own certification audit.
  • NDT personnel certification. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A, certification is issued by an employer under its written practice and ends when employment with that employer ends. Technicians moving to the new company must be certified by the new company, which can use documented prior training, experience and examination results to the extent its own written practice allows.
  • Written practice and procedures. The predecessor's documents can be a starting point, but they must be reissued, approved by the new organization's Level III and matched to the work it intends to do.
  • Records of past work. NDT reports, films and data for hulls and structures built under the previous owner may still be needed by vessel owners and class. Agree in writing who keeps them and for how long.

We help new owners in this position build the NDT side of the program in a sensible order: decide the scope of methods and work, write the written practice, set up the training and certification program, reissue NDT procedures and technique sheets, and recertify people with clean files. Background reading: what SNT-TC-1A certification means and NDT documentation requirements.

Restarting a yard: the first jobs after a quiet spell

A yard that has sat between owners or between contracts tends to lose its NDT readiness quietly. Instruments go past their calibration dates in a locked cabinet, reference blocks and step wedges disappear in the clear-out, penetrant and magnetic particle stock passes its shelf life, and the person who knew where the records were has moved on. None of that shows until the first new job, when an owner's inspector or a class surveyor asks for evidence the yard cannot find.

Before the first hull or module comes in, it pays to walk the NDT store with a checklist. Every instrument either recalibrated or tagged out of service. Every reference standard identified, with its certificate or drawing, or replaced. Consumables checked against batch certificates and expiry dates, with old stock removed. A current list of who may perform and sign each method, with vision checks done. And a records index showing where historic reports and data are kept and under whose control. Our pages on equipment past calibration and calibration records for class work cover the equipment half of that list.

The same walk-through suits an inspection company bidding for the restarted yard's subcontracts. The yard's new quality team will audit its suppliers early, and a company that arrives with a clean evaluation file of its own, written practice, procedures, certifications and calibration register, starts the relationship ahead.

Recycling, dead-ship tows and where NDT fits

Ship recycling is not an NDT-heavy business, and it would be wrong to suggest otherwise. Most of the work is cutting, rigging, handling hazardous materials and managing environmental and worker safety, much of it governed by OSHA's shipyard standards in 29 CFR Part 1915, which cover shipbreaking along with repair and building. Gas-free and hot-work certification by a marine chemist is a safety function, not an NDT one.

Inspection evidence does matter at the edges. Before an inactive vessel is towed from a reserve fleet or layberth to Brownsville, the tow's surveyor and the owner decide whether it is fit for the voyage, and where hull condition is in doubt they may ask for thickness readings or close visual examination of suspect areas. In the yard, heavy lifts of sections depend on lifting points, padeyes and rigging whose welds may be examined before use. Recyclers also run cranes and lifting equipment that need periodic inspection. When a recycler or its contractors do this work, the same rules apply as anywhere: a written procedure, a qualified technician, calibrated equipment and a report that stands up later. The OSHA 1915 shipyard compliance page and its audit preparation checklist cover the overlap between safety rules and NDT records.

Fabrication and construction along the ship channel

Energy construction and offshore fabrication bring owner audits of NDT contractors to the Valley. A terminal or plant owner, or its engineering contractor, will qualify each inspection company before mobilization and audit it during the job. The reviewers typically ask for the written practice, technician certifications with vision checks, procedures for each method and material, demonstration records for any technique used in place of radiography, calibration certificates, and the company's control over its own subcontractors.

Two points catch out firms that are new to large-project work. One is materials: cryogenic service uses austenitic stainless and nickel steels, which need their own UT techniques and controlled penetrant materials, so a carbon-steel procedure set is not enough. The other is radiography. Where the owner's specification calls for RT, a licensed radiography company performs it; Atlantis performs no radiography in the US because of source licensing under 10 CFR Part 34 and the state rules that implement it in Texas. Our Level III can, however, audit the RT company's procedure and review its images on your behalf. For terminal work specifically, see Level III audit support for LNG facilities.

Gauging firms on the lower Texas coast and UR Z17

Barges, workboats and offshore support vessels working the lower Texas coast need hull thickness surveys at drydock and during repairs. When those readings support a class survey, the gauging firm must hold UR Z17 approval from the vessel's classification society. Small firms are common here, and several UR Z17 requirements land hard on them:

  • Operators need at least one year of tutored on-the-job training, and the responsible supervisor at least two years of experience. A one-person firm has to meet the supervisor requirements itself.
  • The firm needs a documented system covering equipment maintenance and calibration and operator training. A system meeting the current ISO 9000 series is accepted as complying, but it is not mandatory.
  • There must be documented work procedures for every service offered, and records for each approved person covering education, training and experience.
  • Approval is conditional on a practical demonstration, and thickness measurement firms are renewed at intervals of no more than three years, shorter than most other service suppliers.
  • Each report carries a copy of the approval certificate.

For a Valley firm the hardest item is usually the first one. Tutored training means a named, qualified person supervised the trainee on real gauging jobs, and the record should show the jobs, the dates and the supervisor's signature. A year of general helper work around a yard does not meet it, and auditors ask to see the log rather than a summary letter.

Our guides to UR Z17 audit preparation, equipment and calibration records and closing UR Z17 findings go into each item, and the UTM operator qualification page deals with operators. The IACS service supplier approval guide covers the whole route, including how each society runs its own scheme.

Records in a bilingual workforce

Many technicians in the Valley trained and work in both Spanish and English. That is a strength on the job, and it raises a records question auditors do ask about. Training outlines, examination papers, procedures and reports must be in a language the auditor and the client can read, and where any of them exist in two languages, the written practice should say which version controls and how translations are checked. If a technician took a practical examination briefed in Spanish, record that, along with who briefed it. The aim is not to discourage either language; it is to make sure nobody later doubts what was taught, tested or reported.

Atlantis's status in the same process

Atlantis is an applicant for class approval, not a holder. Approval under UR Z17 is being sought from Lloyd's Register, DNV and ABS, the audits are still to come, and because no society has issued a certificate, Atlantis has no class approval to offer anyone. The company holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification; it has no ISO/IEC 17020 or 17025 accreditation. It is not an auditor for class, owners or regulators. The employer certifies its NDT staff and owns its procedures, and the auditor reaches its own conclusion; Atlantis helps make the evidence complete.

How we work with Brownsville clients

Atlantis has offices in Houston and Hyderabad and none in the Valley, so most of the work is done by document exchange, with site visits planned around the dates that matter.

  • Scope. We establish which reviews are coming: new-owner program setup, an owner's contractor audit, a class approval application or renewal.
  • Review and drafting. We mark gaps in your documents and records against the governing requirements and draft corrections for your approval.
  • Visit. We sample records, observe examinations or gauging, check equipment against references and run a mock audit.
  • Follow-through. We help prepare corrective actions after the real audit, with evidence attached.

What to send us

  • The audit notice, application form, owner contractor requirements or acquisition timeline.
  • Your current or inherited written practice, procedures and technique sheets.
  • Personnel files for the people to be certified or sampled.
  • Equipment list with calibration certificates.
  • Two or three recent reports, and any earlier audit findings.

Readiness checklist for Valley yards and NDT firms

  • A clear list of which approvals and certificates are held, by whom, and which must be obtained again after any change of ownership.
  • Technicians certified by their current employer under its current written practice.
  • Material-specific procedures for any stainless or nickel steel work.
  • RT subcontractors checked for license, procedure and personnel certification.
  • Gauging records showing tutored training, supervisor experience and daily gauge verification.
  • A stated rule for which language version of each document controls.
  • Certification expiry dates tracked; see expired technician certifications for one approach.

faq.q: We bought a yard. Can the previous owner's class approvals carry over to us?
faq.a: Generally no. An approval names the company the society audited. A new entity applies and is audited in its own name. Ask the society early, because it decides what it will accept as evidence from the predecessor's records.

faq.q: Do technicians who move to us with a yard sale keep their NDT certifications?
faq.a: Not under SNT-TC-1A. Certification is issued by the employer and ends with that employment. Your company certifies them under your written practice, using their documented training, experience and exam history where your practice allows. See SNT-TC-1A certification.

faq.q: Does ship recycling need NDT at all?
faq.a: Occasionally. Tow-fitness decisions, lifting points and crane inspections can call for thickness readings, visual examination or MT. The surveyor or owner decides what evidence is needed; NDT supplies it when asked.

faq.q: Is a small gauging firm with one technician eligible for UR Z17 approval?
faq.a: Yes, in principle, but the one person must meet the supervisor requirements, and all the documented system, procedure, equipment and record requirements still apply. A practical demonstration is part of approval.

faq.q: Does Atlantis hold class approval for thickness measurement?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has UR Z17 applications in progress with ABS, Lloyd's Register and DNV and is preparing for the audits each society will run. No certificate has been issued, so Atlantis holds no class approval.

faq.q: Will Atlantis do radiography on construction jobs at the port?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not do RT work anywhere in the US, because of source licensing. A licensed contractor performs it; Atlantis can audit that contractor's procedure and review the images as a Level III.

faq.q: Can Atlantis be the Level III for a new yard program?
faq.a: Yes. Under SNT-TC-1A or CP-189, an employer may use an outside Level III, and Atlantis can fill that role in the five methods its founder holds (ultrasonic, magnetic particle, penetrant, visual and radiographic), drafting and approving the documents your organization then adopts. More on Level III consulting.

faq.q: Our training is delivered partly in Spanish. Is that a problem for auditors?
faq.a: No, if the records are clear. State in the written practice which language version of each document controls, how translations are checked, and record the language of each training session and examination briefing.

faq.q: Do you design welding procedures for fabrication work?
faq.a: No. Welding procedures and their qualification are the fabricator's responsibility, under its welding engineer. Atlantis works on the NDT program. The WPS and PQR explainer sets out how the two connect.
Send a short description of the audit or the ownership change, with any documents you have, through the contact form. Atlantis answers within one business day.
